full_judgment: 9. Now, let us pass on to the question of possession. It appears that the lower appellate Court, on consideration of both oral and documentary evidence, came to the finding that the defendants could not prove their possession by examining one Obaidul Hoque and one Serajul Hoque through whom defendants were in possession of the suit land. The lower Court did not place any reliance upon the uncorroborated evidence of defendant No.1 to the effect that the defendants were in possession of the disputed land through Obaidul Huq and Serajul Haque as the defendants failed to examine those persons in support of their possession in the disputed land. The lower appellate Court with regard to the statement of DW 2 Mokbul Ali observed that in cross-examination the DW2 admitted that he could not say the name of the cultivators of the suit land. In view of the evidence on record as to possession the lower appellate Court came to the finding that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land. It seems to me that the aforesaid finding is based on solid foundation and I do not find any error of law in reaching such a finding by the lower appellate Court. As from evidence it is found by the lower appellate Court that the opposite party recorded his name in the recent records of right and has been paying rents and are is possession in the entire disputed land. I have no occasion to hold that this finding on possession by the lower appellate Court is not a proper finding of reversal. Although the lower appellate Court found that the opposite party is entitled to the extent of .06 1/2 acres of land out of the entire disputed land but for that matter it cannot be said that the defendants were in ejmali possession of the disputed land with the plaintiff in view of the finding that the plaintiff is in exclusive possession of the disputed land. Therefore the contention of Mr. Karim that plaintiff and the defendants were in ejmali possession and the plaintiff can only retain his possession to the extent of his share i.e. to say in 0.06-1/2 acres of land, can hardly be accepted. The contention must fail. Now let me consider the question as to whether a plaintiff who is a co-sharer in respect of a plot of land and is found in exclusive possession of the entire land can maintain a suit for permanent injunction against the other co-sharers. The paramount consideration which falls for consideration in a suit for permanent injunction is whether the plaintiff has been successful in proving his case of exclusive possession. No doubt the question of title may be looked into incidentally but decision on title in a suit for permanent injunction is not guiding principle for holding that the suit is not maintainable without partition suit. Where a plain-tiff purchases the disputed land from his vendor of which his vendor is a co-sharer only and there are others also co-sharers of the sold land to the plaintiff and where on evidence in suit of permanent injunction it is found that the plaintiff is in exclusive possession of the entire land, I am of the opinion that the suit for permanent injunction is quite maintainable without instituting a suit for partition. It is unfortunate that in this case the lower appellate Court while deciding the suit for permanent injunction entered into the question of title although prima facie on the face of the kabala itself the plaintiff has proved his title, more so when the lower appellate Court itself has observed that the vendor of plaintiff did not challenge the kabala. In this suit the finding regarding title of plaintiff to the extent of 6-1a sataks is irrelevant. However, if the defendants are aggrieved by the transfer in question they have a remedy for redress of their grievance in law in a properly constituted suit for relief or reliefs and to establish their title in the disputed land. In the instant case it has been found by the lower appellate Court that plaintiffs vendor Kamaluddin had 1/4th share in the disputed land but also the lower appellate Court on evidence on record found that the plaintiff was in exclusive possession of the disputed land. Unless and until a suit for partition is instituted, on the face of the finding on possession of the plaintiff arrived at by the lower appellate Court, I hold that the plaintiff can not be evicted from possession of the disputed land to the extent of the share of other co-sharers.
